platforms.title: Ovulation Pain: Why Does Only One Side Hurt Mid-Cycle?
platforms.meta_description: One in five women get one-sided pain at ovulation. What causes mittelschmerz, how many hours it should last, what eases it, and the signs to call a doctor.
platforms.body_html:
Somewhere near the middle of your cycle, nowhere near your period, a low ache shows up on one side of your abdomen and then quietly fades. It has a name: mittelschmerz, German for "middle pain." MedlinePlus, the patient library run by the US National Library of Medicine, puts it plainly: one in five women have pain around the time of ovulation. It is not a sign of disease. But "normal" here comes with a time limit, and knowing that limit is what separates an ordinary cycle from a reason to pick up the phone.

Why One Side, and Why Right Then

Two things happen within a few hours of each other. In the days just before ovulation, the follicle where the egg is developing grows big enough to stretch the surface of the ovary, and MedlinePlus notes that the stretching itself can cause pain. Then the follicle ruptures and releases the egg, and fluid or blood escaping from it can irritate the lining of the abdomen. Cleveland Clinic describes the same two-part picture: both the follicle stretching and the egg bursting through it may be involved.

Only one ovary usually releases an egg in a given cycle, which is why the ache lands on one side rather than across the middle. It may switch sides from month to month, or stay on the same side for many months in a row. There is no blood test for it. A pelvic exam typically shows nothing unusual, and an ultrasound is used mainly to look for other causes of ovarian or pelvic pain, although MedlinePlus notes it can sometimes show a collapsed follicle, which supports the diagnosis.

How Long It Should Last, and Why That Number Is the Whole Ballgame

This is the part worth memorizing. MedlinePlus describes the pain as lasting minutes to a few hours, and at the outside 24 to 48 hours. Cleveland Clinic puts the ceiling in the same place: typically a few hours, up to 48 hours. It begins midway through the menstrual cycle, which for a 28-day cycle lands around day 14, roughly two weeks before the next period starts.

So a one-sided twinge that turns up mid-cycle and is gone by tomorrow fits the ordinary picture. Severe pain that keeps going past a day, gets worse rather than better, or shows up with fever or vomiting does not fit it at all, and that mismatch is your cue to stop waiting it out.

Skip the Guesswork - Here's What Actually Eases It

  • Heat and rest, first - Cleveland Clinic lists a heating pad or a hot bath as reasonable ways to get relief, and most cycles need nothing more than that.
  • An over-the-counter pain reliever if you need one - Cleveland Clinic names ibuprofen, naproxen, or acetaminophen. MedlinePlus adds that pain relievers may be needed when the pain is intense or lasts a long time; most of the time, no treatment is required at all.
  • Hormonal birth control is the only thing that actually prevents it - because it prevents ovulation, and no ovulation means no ovulation pain. Both MedlinePlus and Cleveland Clinic list it for pain bad enough to interfere with normal activities. That is a conversation with your provider, and it also means you will not be able to get pregnant while you take it.
  • Write the date down, but don't plan around it - noting when the pain hits and on which side gives your provider a pattern to work with. Cleveland Clinic is blunt that ovulation pain is not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy; use an actual contraceptive method for that.

One caveat if you are actively trying to conceive. A small controlled study published in Reproductive BioMedicine Online in 2024, run in women undergoing natural-cycle IVF, gave 400 mg of ibuprofen three times a day and found delayed follicle rupture in 22 of 26 participants, against 5 of 25 in the control group. The authors' conclusion was that women trying to conceive should avoid non-selective anti-inflammatory painkillers around the time of ovulation. That is one small study in a fertility-treatment setting rather than general guidance, but if you are trying this cycle, it is worth asking your doctor whether acetaminophen is the better pick that week.

When One-Sided Pain Is Not Mittelschmerz

Cleveland Clinic lists a number of conditions that hurt in exactly the same spot: ovarian cysts, ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, and adhesions from previous abdominal surgery. Call your provider if you missed your last menstrual period, or if the pain arrives with a fever over 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit, pain while urinating, red or burning skin over the painful area, severe nausea or vomiting, heavy vaginal bleeding between periods, or severe mid-cycle pain that lasts longer than a day or turns up during most months. MedlinePlus adds three more triggers: the pain changes character, it lasts longer than usual, or it comes with vaginal bleeding.

If the pain is sudden and severe enough that standing upright is difficult, especially alongside vomiting, treat it as an emergency and call 911 instead of waiting to see whether it passes.

The Bottom Line

If you keep one thing from this page, keep the clock: ovulation pain is measured in hours, and at most a day or two. Heat, rest, and a drugstore painkiller cover the great majority of it; hormonal contraception is the only genuine prevention; and anything that outlasts a day, escalates, or arrives with fever, vomiting, or a missed period belongs in front of a clinician rather than in a waiting game. This article is general health information and not medical advice.
